claims.text: A container image is a reusable, immutable, layered package containing the files, binaries, libraries, and configuration needed to run a container.
A container is an isolated process created and run from an image, and each container is managed independently.
docker run creates and runs a new container from an image; --name assigns a custom identifier and -d runs the container detached.
docker ps lists running containers, and the documented nginx:alpine example shows the labels IMAGE nginx:alpine, STATUS Up, and a custom value under NAMES.
Changes to container state that are not stored persistently disappear when the container is removed.

metadata.description:
Learn the Docker image-versus-container distinction with one nginx:alpine image and two named containers.
See the exact docker run commands, inspect both with docker ps, and understand what persists when a container is removed.

This beginner-friendly Docker Short explains why an image is reusable, why containers are separate isolated instances, and why unstored container changes disappear upon removal.

request.angle: Explain the image/container distinction through a concrete nginx:alpine example. Show two separately named containers started from the same image, then inspect both with docker ps. Use the literal commands and source-supported status labels in the visuals; explain which thing is reusable and which state disappears without persistence.
request.channel_voice_profile: Clear, practical and conversational. Address the viewer directly; use complete sentences, explain unfamiliar terms, avoid hype, unsupported claims and invented personal experience.
notes: Use the exact source-supported example image nginx:alpine. Show docker run --name web-a -d nginx:alpine and docker run --name web-b -d nginx:alpine as two distinct commands; --name values are illustrative identifiers.
Show a compact docker ps display with two rows whose IMAGE is nginx:alpine and NAMES are web-a and web-b. Do not invent container IDs, timestamps, port mappings or an actual execution result.
Explain that the image is the reusable package while each running container is a separate isolated instance.
Clarify that unstored changes disappear after a container is removed. Do not claim that stopping alone deletes them.
Keep display labels literal, short and source-grounded. Reserve the bottom of the portrait frame for captions.

sources.excerpt: A container image packages the files, binaries, libraries and configuration needed to run a container. Docker describes images as immutable and built from layers.
sources.title: Docker Docs: What is an image?

sources.excerpt: Docker describes containers as isolated processes for app components. Each container is independently managed; docker run starts one and docker ps lists running containers.
sources.title: Docker Docs: What is a container?

sources.excerpt: A container is defined by its image and creation or start options. Changes to container state that are not stored persistently disappear when the container is removed.
sources.title: Docker Docs: What is Docker?

sources.excerpt: Docker documents docker run as creating and running a new container from an image. The --name flag assigns a custom identifier, and -d runs detached. Its example is docker run --name test -d nginx:alpine, followed by docker ps showing IMAGE nginx:alpine, STATUS Up, and NAMES test. The example does not publish a host port.

script_sections.narration: One nginx:alpine image can start two separate containers—so what is shared, and what is not?
The image is a reusable package of files, libraries, and configuration. Each container is an isolated process from that image.
Enter docker run --name web-a -d nginx:alpine. Docker starts web-a detached.
Enter docker run --name web-b -d nginx:alpine. Same image, independently managed web-b.
Use docker ps. Both rows show IMAGE nginx:alpine and STATUS Up; NAMES distinguishes web-a from web-b.
The image stays reusable. Each container has separate state, and unstored changes disappear when you remove it. Save this check for your next Docker session.
